summary: We developed an audio and visual based storytelling app that explores the stories and journeys of 11 artefacts scattered across our universe. The journey is guided by Echo, a mysterious friend who mentions his personal investment he has in these stories. Echo moves backward in time starting from the crashed Perseverance descent stage to the historical pioneer rovers. Echo passes by 10 artefacts in his journey and has conversations with some of these abandoned artefacts or explain their significance as they are no longer able to share their stories themselves. Each of our artefacts have their own personalities, weaved by us around what they were, their purpose and how they got to where they are today. This project is important because it transforms cold, hardware technological history into an emotional, character driven narrative. By giving a voice our project has the potential to spark curiosity, builds empathy and interest people into exploring deeper into the universe fascinated by what was discovered in the past.
details:
What it does

Still Out There is a immersive web experience that takes you on a journey backward through time and outward through space to meet the real machines humanity has left scattered across the universe. A forgotten artefact named Echo guides the user as they dive deeper into space.

The UI is scroll driven and glides the user to the next checkpoint via a smooth, cinematic RAF-driven animation. As the user arrive at each artifact they are greeted with a 3D model and a guiding audio (recorded by the team members) which narrates the story or holds a conversation. Captions are synced to improve accessibility and inclusivity.  

The space journey moves through four eras:

  • Mars (2021→1976): Perseverance, InSight, Opportunity, Spirit, Viking 1 — with ambient wind.
  • The Moon (1972→1966): Apollo 17 Rover, Apollo 11 Eagle, Surveyor 1 — in true silence (no atmosphere).
  • Deep space (1977→1972): Voyager 1, Pioneer 11, Pioneer 10 — with a radio-wave hum and intermittent beeps.
  • The reveal/epilogue: Echo is unveiled as Pioneer

 Benefits

  • Accessibility of space history: Transforms dry mission data into an emotional, first-person narrative. Each machine "wakes up just long enough to tell you its story," making the history of planetary exploration feel personal and significant.
  • Educational depth: Each artifact includes a deep-read panel with real mission facts (launch year, distance, power source, status), integrated into the flow without breaking immersion.
  • Captions for accessibility: Full caption support synced to the narration, with distinct speaker labels (ECHO, OPPORTUNITY, VOYAGER 1, etc.), making the experience usable for deaf/hard-of-hearing audiences.
  • No barriers: Runs entirely in a browser. No need for app install, VR headset or plugins. Just open the page and start scroll.

Intended impact

The project aims to reconnect people emotionally with the robotic explorers and portray them as national tresures worth of being talked about, not discarded away like trash. Humanity has sent out many most of which have gone silent, alone in the dark for decades. By giving each machine a voice and a story (Opportunity's last message, Spirit stuck in sand, Voyager still broadcasting 16 billion miles out, Pioneer 10 drifting toward Aldebaran), it fosters:

  • A sense of cosmic perspective visualise how far we've reached, and how fragile and far-away those achievements are.
  • Build inspiration around these machines, they're framed not as hardware but as characters with personalities, fears, and pride.
  • An appreciation for the Golden Record as humanity's message to the unknown. A time capsule still physically playing on a phonograph needle in interstellar space.

Impact on local community

Still Out There is designed to be a free, instantly accessible educational resource for local communities such as schools, libraries, museums, youth STEM programs or even planetariums.

  • Inspiring the next generation: By personifying the spacecraft and telling their stories in an emotional, cinematic way, the experience makes space science feel human rather than a abstract vision. It is effective at sparking curiosity in students who might not see themselves as "science people."
  • No-cost, no-install access: Because it runs in any browser with no downloads or hardware requirements, it reaches under-resourced schools and community centers that can't afford VR headsets, planetarium visits, or specialized software. A library computer is enough.
  • Inclusive design: Full caption support with speaker labels makes the experience usable by deaf and hard-of-hearing community members. The visual 3D models and HUD provide a rich experience even with sound off.
  • Strong cultural connection with the Golden Record which carrys greetings in 55 languages, music from around the world. This is a powerful reminder of humanity's shared culture.
  • Older community members who lived through the Apollo, Viking, and Voyager missions can share their memories while younger viewers discover the history for the first time bridging generations through a shared story we all know.

Tools, languages, and software

  • Framework: Next.js 16 (App Router) with TypeScript, embedded as a fullscreen iframe serving a self-contained HTML experience.
  • 3D rendering: Three.js r128 (CDN) with GLTFLoader and DRACOLoader for the .glb spacecraft/rover models.
  • Audio: HTML5 <audio> elements for narration (recorded human voice, multi-speaker) and the Golden Record; Web Audio API for procedural ambient beds (mars wind, deep-space hum, beeps, vinyl crackle).
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS 4 + shadcn/ui component library.
  • Transcript sync: Silence detection via FFmpeg (silencedetect) to extract precise timecodes; captions distributed proportionally by character count within each segment.
  • Audio processing: FFmpeg for converting/transcoding source recordings (m4a → mp3) and silence analysis; z-ai ASR for transcribing unscripted recordings.
  • Development: Bun runtime, ESLint, Turbopack.
  • Models/audio sources: NASA-derived 3D models and recorded narration provided as project assets.

How it is creative

  • Narrative personification: Each spacecraft speaks in first person with a distinct voice and personality. Opportunity is feisty ("they gave me ninety days. Ninety. I lasted fifteen years"), Spirit is resigned, the Lunar Rover is emotional and energetic("I haven't seen anyone in over fifty years"), Voyager is stoic. Echo acts as a Greek-chorus guide who is himself revealed to be Pioneer 10.
  • Scroll-as-dive metaphor: The entire experience is one continuous scroll creating the sense of "dive" through depth. The user literally descends through space zones, with a checkpoint drift system that turns each scroll gesture into a glide rather than a discrete page jump.
  • Era-driven soundscape: The ambient audio morphs with the era and space. Highlights scientific accuracy through wind on Mars, dead silence on the Moon, radio hum and beeps in deep space.
  • Architectural blending: Real 3D spacecraft models showing what these artifacts looked like on day one before life took them for a ride.
  • The reveal: The guide (Echo) is herself one of the lost machines, a twist mystery that captures the user and reframe the entire journey.

Factors the team considered

  • Sync accuracy: Transcripts are timecoded to the exact speech onset of each audio file (via silence detection), and the caption system was refined so captions appear with the speech rather than drifting early during lead-in silence.
  • Model/audio alignment: Checkpoints and artifact depths were moved to zone centers so the 3D model reaches full opacity exactly when the camera lands, and consecutive models never overlap ("merge") at zone boundaries.
  • Scroll feel: Replaced native scroll-snapping with a custom RAF checkpoint drift — wheel/touch/keyboard each glide to the next artifact, with chaining (continuous scrolling flows through multiple) and reversal (scrolling back mid-glide flips direction).
  • Immersion: Hid the browser scrollbar; moved the Echo indicator to an unobtrusive bottom-left position; suppressed narration during glides so intermediate zones don't stutter.
  • Authenticity: Used real mission facts (heliopause crossing 2012, Opportunity's 28 miles, Viking's biology experiment, the Pioneer plaque); the Golden Record audio is actual Earth sounds.
  • Performance: Models are loaded once and faded per-zone via opacity; the starfield dive speed is derived from the smoothed camera delta so it matches the glide rhythm.
  • Accessibility & inclusion: Captions, browser-only delivery, and low-bandwidth considerations so the experience reaches the widest possible local audience.
  • Extensibility: A documented pipeline (convert audio → public/audio/<id>.mp3, transcript JSON → public/transcripts/<id>.json, .glb → public/models/<id>.glb, then register in MODEL_ZONES
